title: Lesson 8 - A1.4 An Ever-Evolving Threat Landscape (Independent Study)
subject: Information Technology
bigQuestion: How do we stay ahead of cyber threats?

sections.heading: Cyber threats and the threat landscape
sections.text: Cyber security threats are actions or events that try to damage, steal or disrupt computer systems, networks or data. The threat landscape is the whole picture of threats that exist at any time, and it keeps changing.
points: Example: a phishing email tricks someone into clicking a fake link and entering their password
Apply it: a student gets an email saying they've won a free gift and must click a link to claim it
The risk: it's probably phishing, and the link could steal their details or install malware
What to do: don't click, don't reply, report it, and delete it

sections.heading: Why cyber threats keep changing
points: Criminals adapt: from the earliest viruses in the 1970s to today's ransomware, they keep changing their tactics, approaches and targets
Geopolitics changes: conflicts and relations between countries change who attacks whom, and why
New laws and organisations are created to meet new threats
Technology changes: systems become obsolete or get new features, creating new weaknesses, vulnerabilities and things to exploit
Recent example from the slides: ransomware attackers now target backups too, so data resilience is critical
So users, governments and organisations need the latest information to protect their assets

head: Organisation
Where and when
What it does
rows: NCSC: National Cyber Security Centre
UK, launched 2016, supported by GCHQ
Central point of contact and expertise; advice for individuals and organisations of all sizes; news on the latest threats, malware analysis and cybercrime
NIST: National Institute of Standards and Technology
USA, created 1901
Develops cyber security standards and best practice, including the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, used internationally
OWASP: Open Web Application Security Project
Online, non-profit, set up 2001
Improves software security for everyone; not linked to any government; publishes the OWASP Top 10 risks for web apps

sections.heading: NCSC (UK)
points: Launched in 2016 as a central point of contact and expertise for government, organisations and the public
The UK's centre for cyber intelligence, supported by GCHQ (the UK's intelligence, security and cyber agency)
Gives advice and guidance to individuals and organisations of all sizes
Publishes news on the latest threats, malware analysis and recent cybercrime
Your task: complete the NCSC 'Top tips' training and note tips on securing devices, spotting phishing and strong passwords
Standard NCSC advice to note: use three random words for passwords, use a password manager, turn on 2-step verification, install updates, back up your data

sections.heading: NIST (USA)
sections.text: Created in 1901 to support US industry. Its modern role includes developing cyber security standards and best practice.
points: NICE (National Initiative for Cybersecurity Education; your slide says 'Institute'), created 2008, supports government, academic and industry partners
NCCoE (National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence) creates standards-based solutions for all types of organisation
The NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF) is used internationally, so NIST influences security practice worldwide

sections.heading: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework: five core functions
sections.text: Your slides name the five functions. These short meanings are standard explanations to help you remember them:

head: Function
What it means
rows: Identify
Know what you need to protect: your systems, data, people and risks
Protect
Put safeguards in place, e.g. access control, training, updates, encryption
Detect
Spot attacks and unusual activity quickly, e.g. monitoring and logs
Respond
Take action when an incident happens, to contain it and limit damage
Recover
Get systems and data back to normal, e.g. from backups, and learn from it

diagram.alt: The five core functions of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework in order. Identify: know what to protect and the risks. Protect: put safeguards in place. Detect: spot attacks quickly. Respond: act to contain an incident. Recover: restore systems and learn from it, then the cycle repeats.
diagram.caption: Learn them in order: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.

sections.heading: OWASP and the Top 10
sections.text: OWASP is a non-profit online community, set up in 2001 and not linked to any government, focused on improving software security for everyone. The OWASP Top 10 is a live document of the biggest security risks for developers of software and web applications.

head: Risk (2021 list; check owasp.org for the 2025 update)
rows: Broken access control: users can do or see things they shouldn't
Cryptographic failures: sensitive data not encrypted properly
Injection: e.g. SQL injection, where commands typed into a form run on the database
Insecure design: security not planned in from the start
Security misconfiguration: wrong or default settings left in place
Vulnerable and outdated components: old software with known weaknesses
Identification and authentication failures: weak logins and passwords
Software and data integrity failures: trusting updates or data that haven't been checked
Security logging and monitoring failures: attacks not noticed
Server-side request forgery: tricking a server into making requests it shouldn't

sections.heading: Worked example for your OWASP task
sections.text: Task: choose one OWASP Top 10 risk, explain it simply, say why it threatens web security, and find a real example. Here's one done for you, so pick a different one for your own task:
points: Risk: Injection (SQL injection)
What it is: an attacker types database commands into a website's form or search box, and the site runs them
Why it's a threat: the attacker can read, change or delete records in the database, such as customer details
Real example: TalkTalk (2015). Attackers used SQL injection to steal data on around 157,000 customers, and the ICO fined TalkTalk £400,000. Your Lesson 1 links include the ICO's article on it

keyIdea: The threat landscape never stands still: criminals adapt, technology changes and politics shifts. To stay ahead, people and organisations use up-to-date guidance from bodies like the NCSC (UK advice), NIST (the Identify-Protect-Detect-Respond-Recover framework) and OWASP (the Top 10 web risks).

apply.title: Who, what or which function?
apply.intro: Pick the right organisation, NIST function or OWASP risk for each situation.

items.task: A UK small business owner wants free, trusted advice on protecting their company from cyber attacks.
items.e: The NCSC gives UK advice for organisations of all sizes.

items.task: A web developer wants to know the biggest security risks to check for before launching a web app.
items.e: The OWASP Top 10 is aimed at developers of software and web applications.

items.task: An international company wants a recognised framework to organise its whole security approach.
items.e: The NIST CSF is used internationally to improve security practices.

items.task: A company makes a list of all its devices, data and the risks to each. Which NIST function?
items.e: Identify: know what you need to protect and the risks.

items.task: A company installs a firewall, trains staff and turns on 2-step verification. Which NIST function?
Monitoring software alerts the IT team to strange logins at 3am. Which NIST function?
items.e: Detect: spot attacks and unusual activity quickly.

items.task: During an attack, the IT team disconnects infected PCs and tells staff what's happening. Which NIST function?
items.e: Respond: take action to contain an incident and limit damage.

items.task: After a ransomware attack, the company restores its files from backups and reviews what went wrong. Which NIST function?
items.e: Recover: get back to normal and learn from it.

items.task: A website lets attackers type database commands into its search box. Which OWASP risk?
items.e: That's injection (SQL injection), like the TalkTalk attack.

items.task: A normal user changes a number in the web address and can see other customers' orders. Which OWASP risk?
items.e: Users seeing things they shouldn't is broken access control.

items.task: A website still runs a plug-in that hasn't been updated for years and has known weaknesses. Which OWASP risk?
items.e: Old software with known weaknesses is a vulnerable and outdated component.

items.task: Ransomware attackers start deleting backups before encrypting files. What does this show about the threat landscape?
o: Criminals adapt their tactics, so defences must keep up
items.e: Attackers change tactics, which is why up-to-date information matters.

exam.q: 1. Define the term cyber security threat.
pts: An action or event that tries to damage, steal or disrupt
computer systems, networks or data
exam.tip: Two parts: what it tries to do + what it targets.

exam.q: 2. Explain two reasons why cyber threats keep changing.
pts: Cybercriminals adapt their tactics, approaches and targets
so new kinds of attack appear, e.g. ransomware now targeting backups
Technology changes: systems become obsolete or get new features
which creates new weaknesses and vulnerabilities to exploit (also accept: geopolitical changes, new laws)
exam.tip: Two reasons, each with a linked explanation.

exam.q: 3. Describe the role of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC).
pts: The UK's central point of contact and expertise on cyber security, launched in 2016 and supported by GCHQ
Gives advice and guidance to individuals and organisations of all sizes
Publishes news on the latest threats, malware analysis and recent cybercrime
exam.tip: Who it is + who it helps + what it provides.

exam.q: 4. State the five core functions of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework.
pts: Identify
Protect
Detect
Respond
Recover
exam.tip: One mark each. Learn them in order: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.

exam.q: 5. Describe what the OWASP Top 10 is.
pts: A live document listing the biggest security risks
for developers of software and web applications, published by OWASP, a non-profit organisation
exam.tip: What it is + who it's for.

exam.sc: Bloom Florists is a small UK business with 8 staff. It sells flowers through a website that a freelancer built three years ago and hasn't updated since. The owner knows cyber attacks are increasing but doesn't know where to start. There is no plan for what to do if the business is attacked, and backups are rarely checked.
exam.q: 6. Recommend which organisation's guidance Bloom Florists should use to check its website, and explain why.
pts: OWASP: use the OWASP Top 10
because it lists the biggest risks for web applications, and Bloom's website hasn't been updated in three years (e.g. outdated components)

exam.sc: Bloom Florists is a small UK business with 8 staff. It sells flowers through a website that a freelancer built three years ago and hasn't updated since. The owner knows cyber attacks are increasing but doesn't know where to start. There is no plan for what to do if the business is attacked, and backups are rarely checked.
exam.q: 7. Explain how Bloom Florists could use two functions of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework to improve its security.
pts: Function 1, e.g. Respond
write a plan for what to do if attacked, because Bloom currently has none, so damage is limited
Function 2, e.g. Recover
check backups regularly so the website and data can be restored after an attack (also accept Identify, Protect or Detect with a scenario link)
exam.tip: Pick functions that fix Bloom's actual problems (no plan, unchecked backups, outdated website).

exam.sc: Bloom Florists is a small UK business with 8 staff. It sells flowers through a website that a freelancer built three years ago and hasn't updated since. The owner knows cyber attacks are increasing but doesn't know where to start. There is no plan for what to do if the business is attacked, and backups are rarely checked.
exam.q: 8. Evaluate how useful organisations such as the NCSC, NIST and OWASP are to a small business like Bloom Florists.
pts: Strength: NCSC gives free, UK-focused advice for organisations of all sizes, ideal for an owner who doesn't know where to start
Strength: they track the changing threat landscape, so Bloom gets up-to-date information
Strength: the NIST CSF gives a clear structure (Identify to Recover), and OWASP shows what to check on the website
Weakness: guidance only helps if someone acts on it; a small business may lack the time, skills or money
Weakness: NIST is US-based and fairly technical, so it may be less suited to a small UK business than the NCSC
Justified conclusion: very useful, especially the NCSC, but Bloom still needs to act, e.g. update the website and test backups
exam.tip: Top-grade "evaluate" = strengths AND weaknesses, linked to Bloom, then a clear judgement.
